abstract: Genetically identical microbial cells often differ in their growth rate and metabolic state, and in how long they take to resume growth after a shift of conditions. Preparing for uncertain future conditions is costly: cells that allocate part of their proteome to a future nutrient grow more slowly on the present one. Bet hedging offers a complementary strategy: a genotype whose cells occupy different metabolic states makes it likely that some of them are suited to whatever condition follows and resume growth quickly. Here, we investigate when phenotypic variability in metabolic allocation can outperform the evolutionary stable homogeneous strategy, in which all cells share the same allocation. We consider serial-dilution cultures, where each cycle ends when the nutrient is exhausted, and fluctuations in dilution or nutrient supply change the fold increase in biomass required in each cycle, i.e., the growth factor. We identify two distinct mechanisms by which selection can favor phenotypic heterogeneity. First, noise in the growth factor leaves the optimal mean allocation unchanged but can destabilize the homogeneous strategy: cycles that demand much growth favor fast growers, whereas cycles that demand little growth favor well-prepared cells. Variability in allocation is therefore favored above a critical noise level, set by the mean logarithm of the growth factor and by how steeply the lag increases as the allocation to the incoming nutrient decreases. Second, with multiple possible future nutrients, different cells can allocate their proteome to different future nutrients. When the lag is sufficiently long relative to the growth time, an all-in strategy, in which cells specialize in individual future nutrients, is favored independently of noise in the growth factor. Invasion analysis of narrow phenotypic distributions shows that these two mechanisms define four evolutionary regimes, confirmed by competition and evolution simulations. Our results show how environmental uncertainty can make cell-to-cell variability selectively advantageous, so that evolution acts on the distribution of phenotypes within a genotype, not only on its mean.
